name: Science for Every Student
title: Science for Every Student
answer: Science for Every Student means using AI to adapt the same science investigation so students with different reading levels, languages, and needs can all take part. It matters because the goal is full participation in real science, not a watered down version. Teachers still review every adapted material before the lab.

sections.body: Science classes often bring together students who read at different levels, speak different languages, and have different needs. AI can help a teacher prepare materials that remove barriers while keeping the investigation itself unchanged. A lab procedure might be rewritten in simpler steps with pictures, translated into a student's home language, or read aloud with a tool such as Microsoft Immersive Reader. The problem it solves is that the science can stay the same for everyone even when the supports differ. This lets more students join the same inquiry rather than sit apart from it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a science lab, a teacher can use AI to create a short vocabulary list with pictures and simple definitions for terms such as variable, hypothesis, and evidence. English learners can study that list before the lab and use it during the lab and when writing up results, and the text notes that native English speakers also benefit because science vocabulary is hard in any language. For students with disabilities, the adjustments may be different. A student with a fine motor disability might record observations by voice instead of writing, and a student who struggles with organization might use a step by step checklist generated for the lab. The text does not give grade bands, so these examples apply across science classes where labs and investigations happen.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no study, figure, or evidence label for this idea. It presents the approach as practice, with examples of adapted procedures, vocabulary lists, voice recording, and checklists rather than research findings. So this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Every adapted material needs a teacher's check before it is used. Simplified procedures can drop a safety step, and translations can garble a technical term, so a quick review protects students and keeps the science accurate. For students with disabilities, the individualized education program team and the science teacher decide which supports fit each student. The text also says that time saved matters only if the result is right. The decisions about safety, accuracy, and individual supports stay with people, not with the AI.
